newsitem.title: USA: Still no U.S.-EU meat deal, but maybe some progress.
newsitem.headline: Still no U.S.-EU meat deal, but maybe some progress.

text.p: U.S. and European Union officials were unable this week to settle a trade dispute over meat imports, but senior negotiators said some progress had been made in the difficult talks and they were not giving up.

After meeting in Washington late into Wednesday night and again Thursday morning, EU officials headed back to Brussels, Belgium. Negotiators said they would continue to communicate and held out the possibility of more face-to-face talks next week, perhaps in Brussels.

"It was a constructive meeting, with as usual some bumps in the road, but some progress was made," said senior U.S. negotiator Paul Drazek. "We narrowed the differences overall this past week, but the differences aren't gone."

"We have had progress, but we have also perhaps had some setbacks," said head EU negotiator Lars Hoelgaard. Hoelgaard said he had hoped the dispute would be settled this week and that he was "somewhat disappointed" at the outcome.

Officials have been trying to resolve a long-running dispute between the United States and the European Union over meat import inspection regulations. An agreement would allow each side to buy meat and poultry products from the other if their safety inspection and processing methods differ.

The failure to reach an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks has already disrupted U.S. poultry shipments to Europe, worth some $50 million a year, and threatens to halt more than $300 million worth of European meat exports to the United States by the end of the month.
Washington has threatened to remove over 100 European meat and poultry plants from its list of approved exporters on April 30 and stop meat imports if the dispute has not been resolved by then.
The key sticking point of the talks has been the U.S. poultry industry's use of chlorine as a decontaminant in the slaughter process, which the European Union opposes.
Hoelgaard indicated some easing in that area. "The question of decontamination has become less acute," he said.
But Drazek said the issue of decontamination remains a "major problem and still a concern."
"The use of antimicrobial treatments (in poultry) is still an issue between us," he said.
Hoelgaard told reporters at a briefing that another unresolved area is that of so-called regionalization, and how the United States recognises animal health status in the EU.
Drazek expressed some surprise that this issue had been raised again. He said U.S. officials thought the issue had been resolved some time ago.
Drazek said Europe wants Washington to treat the EU as one entity, and that U.S. officials said they would do as much as they can "in the scope of our statutes and regulations."

Hoelgaard repeated warnings that if Washington halts European meat imports at the end of the month, it would only worsen the already tense situation and would "trigger appropriate action on our side."
